name: Commercialization Timing

positioning.oneLineSummary: Separates technical readiness, ecosystem readiness, customer readiness, and commercialization capability to test whether now is a viable time.
positioning.productLabel: Commercialization Timing Lens — based on Marc Andreessen's public timing essays and talks
notAClaimOf: a previously failed idea now being timely

attribution.display: Based on Marc Andreessen's public timing essays and talks

neutralParaphrase: Assess timing across independent clocks: the core technology must work at an acceptable cost and reliability, the ecosystem and society must permit adoption, customers must react to a real offer, and the team must be able to commercialize before capital or competitive time runs out.

locator.value: Lines 116-137: recurring ideas and technology, social, first-customer, and commercialization timing questions
PDF pp. 16-18: timing, technology, market, distribution, and financing risk layers
Lines 95-122: official episode description on platform shifts and why being too early resembles being wrong

requiredConditions: The product depends on at least one uncertain technical, ecosystem, customer, regulatory, or commercialization clock.
Readiness claims are dated and geography-specific.
The analysis distinguishes a good idea from a timely investable company.

requiredEvidence.description: Performance, reliability, cost, manufacturability, integration, safety, and remaining technical dependencies.
Infrastructure, complements, standards, supply chain, regulation, buyer workflow, and social acceptance.
Real customer reaction, adoption friction, procurement path, budget, willingness to pay, and switching behavior.
Sales, distribution, capital runway, competitive entry, and time required to reach repeatability.

decisionQuestions: Which readiness clock is currently the binding constraint?
What observable event would show that clock has advanced?
Can the company survive financially until the clocks align?
Can competitors exploit the same platform shift sooner?
What evidence distinguishes being early from being technically or commercially wrong?
positiveSignals: Technical performance crosses a customer-relevant cost or reliability threshold.
Required infrastructure, standards, channels, and regulation are becoming available.
Real customers adopt under realistic pricing and workflow conditions.
The company has a financed sequence of milestones to bridge remaining timing gaps.
redFlags: The timing thesis rests on a prior failed attempt becoming fashionable again.
A lab result is treated as proof of deployability or willingness to pay.
The ecosystem depends on uncommitted partners or unpassed regulation.
The company will exhaust capital before a critical readiness milestone.
disconfirmingEvidence: A small niche may be ready even when the mass market is not.
A regulated market may have strong committed demand despite slow deployment.
A technically inferior product may commercialize sooner through superior distribution.
A platform shift may lower barriers for competitors as well as the company.
contraindications: Do not use current sector funding as a proxy for customer timing.
Do not infer that persistence across historical attempts proves the current team is right.
Do not turn timing conviction into a valuation premium without scenario analysis.

instructions: Map the technical, ecosystem, customer, regulatory, commercialization, capital, and competitive clocks.
Identify the binding clock and evidence threshold for readiness.
Estimate the sequence and duration of remaining milestones.
Compare that sequence with runway and competitor timing.
Conclude aligned, plausibly bridging, too early, too late, wrong mechanism, or insufficient.

sourceReliability.high: Independent technical, ecosystem, customer, and contractual evidence converge.

evidenceStrength.medium: One or two clocks show readiness.
evidenceStrength.high: Binding clocks are crossed or credibly financed with real customer validation.

evidenceCoverage.high: All clocks, dependencies, runway, competition, and counterevidence covered.

judgmentConfidence.high: Current readiness evidence and milestone timing converge.

empiricalQualifications: Timing judgments have strong hindsight bias.
Platform shifts can benefit incumbents or competitors instead.

rights.notes: Author-direct public timing material is neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Add sector-specific clock templates and failed-case review.
